title: Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge
abstract: Policy AI Report Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge At a moment when voters are fearful of AI, Democrats are finding their footing. by Lauren Feiner Oct 19, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photo by Stephen Morton, Getty Images Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI. Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on tax credits tied to data centers and recent hacking incidents , and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings. AI issues are already taking a leading role in campaign ads, particularly as data center development has driven residents across the political spectrum to packed local meetings. While President Donald Trump has opposed most regulation of the technology in favor of an accelerationist approach, public opinion polling has shown that Americans have widespread concerns about how AI will impact jobs, education, and other aspects of life. The direction and intensity of that oversight, though, is up for grabs. The issue of AI is “a hundred percent ready for the taking,” says Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist who previously ran a tech accountability advocacy group and worked for Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. “The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity.” AI issues currently include a lot of different things, from monitoring and restricting the development of frontier models to dealing with the effects of job displacement or data centers’ energy demands. Across both parties, lawmakers are still figuring out where to put their stakes in the ground, and early congressional proposals have yet to gain broad consensus. “The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity” AI caught many lawmakers off guard, says Rob Flaherty, former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign and a Biden White House alum who cohosts a podcast with Lehrich. “For a long time, Democrats were afraid to talk about it, either for a mix of not understanding it, or being afraid of the money that was going to be poured in by the AI industry,” Flaherty says. But as AI becomes more salient for voters, “there will be immense profit to whoever can speak to the world that we’re moving into at a volume that voters can hear and can feel.” Flaherty recently launched a super PAC called Tomorrow Together with Karthik Ganapathy, a former state communications director for Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign. The group launched its first $4 million ad blitz last week in battleground House races, attacking Republican candidates as out of touch on AI and referencing issues like kids’ online safety and data centers. The group is looking beyond the midterms toward the 2028 presidential election, aiming to hone Democrats’ messaging to double down on what resonates most with voters. While data centers have been the most visible AI issue in many communities, Flaherty says his group’s polling found sweeping bans on state AI regulation — repeatedly pushed by Trump and congressional Republicans — are even more broadly unpopular. Democratic donor and venture capitalist Ron Conway now regrets funding Marc Andreessen-backed pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, Jay Carney, a former Obama press secretary who now runs communications for Conway’s VC fund, told Politico . As of June, LTF spent nearly $45 million over almost a year, with $31 million left in the pot according to Federal Election Commission filing s. “At a certain point, voters speak louder than money,” Flaherty says. Even governors who lean toward the center of the Democratic Party, like California’s Gavin Newsom or Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, have taken bolder stances against AI in recent weeks. Newsom issued an executive order looking to create an AI “kill switch” after previously vetoing a bill that would have instituted some similar measures, and Shapiro reversed course against data centers . Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI because Trump’s largely anti-regulation stance has boxed in his party. Though some Republicans, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), have carved out a more skeptical approach to AI, Lehrich says, “I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry and declaring that we must let data reign and any community that rejects data centers is backwards and poor.” A more sweeping AI regulatory agenda might include embedding independent researchers into frontier labs, requiring more safety checks up front, and imposing more liability on tech companies for anything from how their tools affect kids to whether they’re used to discriminate against workers or housing applicants. Lawmakers could also consider ways to meet demands from constituents that AI companies help pay for job displacement and other impacts they’ll have on people’s lives. “I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry” AI is still not the top issue driving voters to the polls, but Flaherty says that’s not necessarily the right way to think about it. “AI is not an issue as much as it is a story,” he says. “It’s a story of politicians getting bought off by industry. It’s a story of a bunch of guys making you foot the bill for them getting rich while they’re coming to make your life worse. It is a story that fits the national vibe.” Where exactly different policy lines should be drawn on AI is still somewhat unsettled. But Flaherty warns that Democrats risk giving up ground if they fail to take big enough swings. Voters are “giving politicians a lot of leeway to take big swings and to really reimagine stuff,” he says. If politicians only stick to basics like plans to retrain workers at community colleges, “I think we’re going to miss the bigness and the ingenuity that the moment calls for.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: A woman was arrested in Philly for blocking a delivery robot
abstract: AI News Policy A woman was arrested in Philly for blocking a delivery robot Carolyn Marvin was charged with ‘disorderly conduct’ for protesting delivery robots taking jobs. Carolyn Marvin was charged with ‘disorderly conduct’ for protesting delivery robots taking jobs. by Terrence O'Brien Oct 18, 2026, 6:28 PM UTC Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. Carolyn Marvin was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct after blocking the path of an Uber delivery robot and refusing to get out of the way. Marvin told Philadelphia’s ABC13 “I know they’re taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward.” Police responded to the scene and asked Marvin to move out of the robot’s way. When she refused, they placed her in cuffs and arrested her. The incident was captured on video and has now garnered considerable media attention. The delivery robots have become a common sight on the streets of downtown Philadelphia and have sparked backlash. This is not even Marvin’s first brush with them. And earlier this year, one was kicked over in Center City. Broad concern has grown about how autonomous systems, including robotaxis, delivery robots, and AI agents, are impacting jobs, especially for lower-skill workers . MiniMax Just Launched M3.1 Flash: 428B MoE Agentic Model at $0.15/M Input
abstract: MiniMax has just released MiniMax M3.1 Flash on its API, priced at $0.15 per 1M input tokens . MiniMax also confirmed that Space Bunny was an earlier M3.1 Flash build. That stealth model processed over 200T tokens. For developers, the message is near-frontier agentic scores at Flash-tier cost. Model weights are due in late October, 2026. MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model from MiniMax. It targets coding, agentic office work and visual reasoning. MiniMax’s product page lists 428B total parameters and about 23B active. It also mentions sparse attention and a native visual encoder. The model accepts text, image and video input and returns text. The context window is 1,000,000 tokens. Those parameter totals match MiniMax M3 , which ships at ~428B total and ~23B active. MiniMax has not published a technical report on what changed in the Flash variant. Reasoning is always on and cannot be disabled. Developers choose from 5 effort levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. MiniMax recommends Max as the default. Migration matters here. Requests sending thinking.type=disabled or effort=none return an error. Reasoning arrives in a separate reasoning_content field, which may be absent. Integrations that parse inline <think> tags from M3 need updating. All scores below are MiniMax-reported. No independent replication exists yet. On the CoWork set, M3.1 Flash leads Automation-Bench v1.0.6 at 62.2 . Opus 5 scores 50.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol 45.8. It ties Opus 5 on BankerToolBench at 76.2. It also tops LOCA-Bench 256K at 60.3. Agents’ Last Exam lands at 29.6. Coding results are mixed. DeepSWE v1.1 scores 73.7, just above GPT-5.6 Sol at 73.0. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 scores higher at 77.0. Terminal Bench 4.0 is the weakest result at 38.1. SWE Refactor Bench sits at 23.0, versus 31.0 for Opus 5. On vision, BabyVision with tools reaches 91.0 and CharXiv RQ reaches 82.5. HLE without tools scores 43.4. Spot checks hold up. The Kimi K3 model card reports DeepSWE 67.5 and BabyVision 85.7, matching MiniMax’s table. One inconsistency: MiniMax’s cost chart plots Automation-Bench max effort at 62.8, while its table says 62.2. MiniMax frames value as cost per task, not per token. On its Automation-Bench chart, all 5 effort levels sit below $0.05 per task. Scores range from 52.8 at low effort to 62.8 at max. A full 152-task Agents’ Last Exam run cost about $111 at 29.6. On DeepSWE, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 plots both higher and cheaper at max effort. The model is live on platform.minimax.io as MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . MiniMax supports Anthropic-compatible and OpenAI-compatible access, including Chat Completions and Responses. It is also available through M Plan and the MiniMax Code desktop app . Pricing is a flat $0.15 input and $0.60 output per 1M tokens. Cache reads cost $0.015 per 1M. There is no long-context surcharge. MiniMax M3 costs $0.30/$1.20 up to 512K input and doubles above that. Per token, Flash is half of M3’s standard rate. MiniMax claims 1/3 the cost of M3 but has not detailed the calculation. On speed, MiniMax’s product page lists about 150 tokens per second. The announcement claims 3x the speed of M3. Weights arrive October 23; the license is not yet disclosed. For scale, M3’s MXFP8 build is about 440 GB . *Scores from MiniMax’s comparison table . Kimi K3 DeepSWE and BabyVision match its own card. Every benchmark is vendor-reported, and harness choice shifts results. Automation-Bench numbers do not transfer across sources. Kimi K3’s card reports 30.8 on a 600-task public subset, while MiniMax lists 46.7. Opus 5 leads by 13.7 points on Terminal Bench 4.0 and 14.1 on NL2Repo-Bench. Always-on reasoning also sets a token and latency floor for simple calls. Self-hosting details remain unknown until October 23. Check out the announcement , product page and API docs . title: NVIDIA Open Sources Run:ai Under Apache 2.0 for Kubernetes GPU Orchestration
abstract: NVIDIA has released the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform as open source software. The source code ships under the Apache 2.0 license on GitHub. NVIDIA Run:ai open source puts production GPU scheduling, quotas and workload management in developers’ hands. The release, makes Run:ai part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. Platform teams can now inspect, fork and self-host the stack without a paid subscription. NVIDIA Run:ai is an AI workload and GPU orchestration platform for Kubernetes from NVIDIA. It schedules development, training and inference workloads across shared GPU clusters. It runs on top of Kubernetes and does not replace it. The control plane handles workload submission, resource management and monitoring. Cluster services run on each Kubernetes cluster and add GPU-aware scheduling. Users reach it through a web UI, CLI, REST API and an MCP server for AI assistants. NVIDIA split the release into 4 components that teams can adopt independently: The local development guide stands on 1 script, local-dev.sh . It builds about 50 Go services from source inside containers. It then creates a 5-node Kind cluster pinned to Kubernetes v1.32.5. A fake GPU operator simulates 8 Tesla-A10 GPUs, so no GPU hardware is required. The --gpu-operator flag switches to real NVIDIA GPUs. That mode needs Linux, Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. AMD and Intel accelerators are not supported. Dev teams can deploy from source or from the NGC Community Product Helm chart. That edition needs no paid subscription but excludes NVIDIA enterprise support. Teams can also adopt it through 8 DSX ecosystem partners. These are Crusoe , Mirantis , Nebius , OpenNebula Systems , Rafay , Saturn Cloud , Spectro Cloud and vCluster . Supported commercial editions continue through NVIDIA AI Enterprise, NVIDIA Mission Control and select cloud marketplaces. Two adjacent projects round out the stack. Model Streamer streams model weights directly into GPU memory. vLLM and SGLang enable it with --load-format runai_streamer . Microsoft’s published benchmark used 8 NVIDIA H100 VMs. It showed 3x to 6x faster loading than the default loader. Throughput held at 80 Gbps versus about 40 Gbps on the default path. Grove orchestrates multicomponent inference workloads. It starts components such as prefill and decode as all-or-nothing units. The key difference is scope. Volcano, Kueue and YuniKorn focus on scheduling or queueing. Run:ai ships a full management platform on top of its scheduler. Check out the GitHub repo , the local dev guide and NVIDIA’s technical blog . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: Mistral AI Releases Timestral: A 209M Forecasting Model Family That Outperforms Google’s TimesFM-3
abstract: Mistral AI has released Timestral , its first family of time series foundation models. Timestral is a set of 4 zero-shot forecasting models from Mistral AI, sized from 5M to 209M parameters. The largest checkpoint ranks first among pretrained, zero-shot models on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. It does this without a GPU at inference. For developers, this Timestral time series foundation model means probabilistic forecasts on standard server CPUs, with open weights and inference code . Timestral is a time series foundation model (TSFM). It is pretrained on a large, diverse corpus, then forecasts zero-shot on data it has never seen. Classical tools like ARIMA fit one series at a time. Deep models like PatchTST usually train from scratch on each dataset. Timestral transfers patterns across domains instead. Each model outputs 21 quantiles per time step . It forecasts multivariate targets jointly. It accepts past-only, known-future and categorical covariates. Timestral is a causal, patch-based transformer with time attention and variate attention. The 209M model uses 24 layers and an embedding dimension of 768 . Each patch covers 32 time steps. A single forward pass forecasts up to 1,024 steps. Longer horizons run block by block, feeding each block’s median back as context. Mistral lists 4 technical contributions : All scores below are zero-shot, from a single checkpoint without ensembling. They come from the Timestral-209M model card . The size scaling is flat at the top. Timestral-123M scores 0.659 MASE on GIFT-Eval , against 0.658 for 209M. Mistral team states that the 28M model beats Chronos-2 on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Chronos-2 is about 4 times larger. Mistral team tested a standard server CPU with 8 threads. The task: forecast 1 day ahead from 3 weeks of 15-minute history. The 5M model took 10 ms and the 209M model took 140 ms . The 28M model is 5 times faster than 209M. The 123M model lands within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency. * As listed on the Timestral-209M model card . Google and Amazon do not publish matching figures on their own model pages. ** From Datadog’s model card . Mistral’s card lists 0.642 / 0.539. Install the package with pip install git+https://github.com/mistralai/timestral.git . It needs Python 3.10+ and torch 2.4+ . Dependencies are PyTorch, NumPy, safetensors and huggingface_hub. Weights download from Hugging Face: 21 MB for 5M, 111 MB for 28M, 490 MB for 123M . Mistral’s docs list Timestral 1.0 209M as Public Preview . Fine-tuning on proprietary data runs through Mistral Forge . The pipeline can deploy on-prem, in a VPC or air-gapped. Check out the blog post , GitHub repo and model weights on Hugging Face . title: Claude Haiku 5.5: What’s New and How to Use It for Fast, Cheap AI Workflows
abstract: Claude Haiku 5.5: What’s New and How to Use It for Fast, Cheap AI Workflows Claude Haiku 5.5 cuts list prices by 90% and adds adaptive thinking and a 1M token context window. Learn what broke from Haiku 4.5, and build classification, extraction, and sub-agent workflows in Python using the new API. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 19, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, and calls it its cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model. The API model ID is claude-haiku-5-5 , and prompts up to 100,000 tokens cost \$0.10 per million input tokens and \$0.50 per million output tokens. This article covers what changed since Haiku 4.5, how to build fast, cheap AI workflows with it in Python (classification, extraction, and sub-agents), and when a bigger Claude model is still the better pick. Haiku 5.5 Anthropic positions Haiku 5.5 for high-volume, cost-sensitive work such as summaries, compaction, database queries, and classification, and as a subagent alongside Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. It is available on the Claude Platform, Amazon Web Services , Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Its safety evaluations are documented in the system card . Anthropic's deprecation page lists the earliest retirement date as October 7, 2027. What's New Compared With Haiku 4.5? Feature Haiku 4.5 Haiku 5.5 Context window 200K tokens 1M tokens Max output 64K tokens 128K tokens Thinking control Manual thinking budget Adaptive thinking with an effort setting, a first for a Haiku Price per million tokens, prompts up to 100K (input / output) \$1.00 / \$5.00 \$0.10 / \$0.50 Price over 100K \$1.00 / \$5.00 \$0.50 / \$2.50 Smallest cacheable prompt 4,096 tokens 512 tokens GDPval-AA (knowledge work) 735 1620 OSWorld 2.1, offline subset (computer use) 15.7% 72.4% Humanity's Last Exam, no tools 10.2% 45.9% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (agentic coding) 0.0% 39.2% The benchmark rows are Anthropic's own results, and the launch page shows Sonnet 5.5 ahead on all four (for example, 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0). The price cut is also smaller in practice than the list prices suggest. Haiku 5.5 uses a newer tokenizer, so the same text counts as roughly 30% more tokens . Anthropic puts the average saving at around 75% , after accounting for the tokenizer and for the 10% of requests that run over 100K tokens. Three changes can break existing Haiku 4.5 code. The what's-new page lists them as breaking: sending temperature , top_p , or top_k returns an error, ending the messages with an assistant prefill returns an error, and manual thinking with budget_tokens returns an error. Two behavior changes matter as well. Adaptive thinking is on by default, so a response can start with a thinking block, and thinking tokens count toward max_tokens . Safety classifiers can also decline a request, so your code must handle stop_reason: "refusal" . On safety, Anthropic says Haiku 5.5's cybersecurity safeguards are stricter than Haiku 4.5's and block penetration testing. Using Haiku 5.5 for Fast, Cheap Workflows You need Python 3.10 or newer, an API key from the Claude Console, and a recent Anthropic SDK, since the code below uses the newer output_config parameter. pip install -U anthropic export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key-here" The first command installs or upgrades the official Python SDK. The second stores your key in the shell session, and the SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY automatically. On Windows PowerShell, use $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key-here" . Step 1: Classification and Extraction These are the two jobs Haiku was built for: a short input and a short, structured answer, repeated thousands of times. The code uses JSON outputs, which constrain the reply to a schema you provide. It also holds the shared price table and a cost helper that the next two scripts reuse. # haiku_tasks.py """Fast, cheap Claude Haiku 5.5 calls: classification and extraction with JSON outputs.""" import json import anthropic MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5" client = anthropic.Anthropic() # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment # USD per million tokens (input, output) for prompts up to 100K tokens. PRICES = { "claude-haiku-5-5": (0.10, 0.50), "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00), "claude-opus-5-5": (4.00, 20.00), } CATEGORY_SCHEMA = { "type": "object", "properties": {"category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "shipping", "technical", "other"]}}, "required": ["category"], "additionalProperties": False, } INVOICE_SCHEMA = { "type": "object", "properties": { "vendor": {"type": "string"}, "invoice_number": {"type": "string"}, "total": {"type": "number"}, "currency": {"type": "string"}, "due_date": {"type": "string", "description": "ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD"}, }, "required": ["vendor", "invoice_number", "total", "currency", "due_date"], "additionalProperties": False, } def cost_usd(model, usage): price_in, price_out = PRICES[model] return (usage.input_tokens * price_in + usage.output_tokens * price_out) / 1_000_000 def ask_json(schema, instruction, text, model=MODEL, effort="low"): """One request whose reply must be JSON matching `schema`. Returns (data, usage).""" reply = client.messages.create( model=model, max_tokens=1000, # thinking tokens count toward this limit, so leave headroom system=instruction, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}], output_config={"effort": effort, "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}}, ) if reply.stop_reason in ("refusal", "max_tokens"): raise RuntimeError(f"No usable answer, stop reason: {reply.stop_reason}") # A reply can start with a thinking block, so pick the text block by type. answer = "".join(block.text for block in reply.content if block.type == "text") return json.loads(answer), reply.usage def classify(text, model=MODEL): data, usage = ask_json(CATEGORY_SCHEMA, "Classify the customer message.", text, model) return data["category"], usage def extract_invoice(text, model=MODEL): data, usage = ask_json(INVOICE_SCHEMA, "Extract the invoice fields from the text.", text, model) return data, usage if __name__ == "__main__": for message in ["I was charged twice this month.", "My parcel never arrived.", "The app crashes on login."]: category, usage = classify(message) print(f"{category:<10} {usage.input_tokens} in / {usage.output_tokens} out <- {message}") invoice = "Acme Cloud Ltd, invoice AC-2291. Total due: 1,240.50 USD by 15 November 2026." fields, usage = extract_invoice(invoice) print(fields, f"(${cost_usd(MODEL, usage):.6f})") PRICES lists input and output prices per million tokens for the three models (from Anthropic's launch page and pricing page ), and cost_usd turns a response's token counts into dollars. The two schemas describe the output you want: CATEGORY_SCHEMA limits category to four allowed values, and INVOICE_SCHEMA lists five fields. ask_json is the core function. It sends one request with the schema inside output_config.format , and effort set to low , so the model spends little time thinking on an easy task. Anthropic's JSON outputs guarantee valid JSON that matches the schema. Notice what is missing: there is no temperature , because Haiku 5.5 rejects it. max_tokens is 1000 even though answers are tiny, since thinking tokens count against it. Two checks follow. A stop reason of refusal or max_tokens raises an error instead of failing silently on a half-empty reply. Then the text is read by block type, because a reply may begin with a thinking block, and parsed as JSON. I used JSON outputs instead of forcing a tool call on purpose. Haiku 5.5 accepts a forced tool call , but Opus 5.5 rejects one with a 400 error , so JSON outputs are the portable choice for the three-model comparison in Step 3. One caveat: JSON outputs are not available on Amazon Bedrock for Haiku 5.5, so on Bedrock you describe the format in the prompt and validate the result yourself. Run it: python haiku_tasks.

title: LangChain vs. LlamaIndex vs. Building From Scratch: Here’s What I Suggest
abstract: LangChain vs. LlamaIndex vs. Building From Scratch: Here’s What I Suggest Choosing the right framework for your large language model application comes down to one question: what are you actually optimizing for? By Vinod Chugani on October 19, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence The tooling ecosystem around large language models (LLMs) has expanded faster than most practitioners can track. Two names dominate nearly every conversation about LLM application development: LangChain and LlamaIndex . Both promise to reduce the friction of building with LLMs. Both have large communities and active development. And both get recommended, almost reflexively, the moment someone asks how to get started. But neither one is the right answer for every team, every project, or every stage of development. A third path is increasingly worth serious consideration: building from scratch, using nothing but the base APIs and your own abstractions. This guide breaks down what each approach actually offers, where each one creates problems, and how to decide which path fits your situation. The goal isn't to crown a winner. It's to help you make a deliberate choice rather than defaulting to whatever has the most GitHub stars. Understanding What These Tools Actually Do Before comparing them, it helps to be precise about the problem they solve. LLMs on their own are stateless text predictors. They take a prompt, return a completion, and remember nothing. Building useful applications on top of them — things like document question-answering systems, multi-step agents, retrieval pipelines, or conversational interfaces — requires orchestration: managing context, routing between tools, retrieving relevant information, handling memory, and chaining operations together. LangChain and LlamaIndex both provide that orchestration layer. They abstract away the plumbing so developers can focus on application logic rather than infrastructure. Building from scratch means writing that plumbing yourself. LangChain: Broad, Flexible, Occasionally Overwhelming LangChain arrived early and built an enormous surface area. Its strength is breadth. It provides abstractions for chains, agents, memory, tools, retrievers, output parsers, prompt templates, and dozens of integrations with external services, databases, and APIs. Where It Works Well Teams that need to connect LLMs to a wide variety of external tools and data sources will find LangChain's integration library genuinely useful. It covers a remarkable range of providers — from vector databases to search engines to custom APIs — and the community has produced extensive documentation and examples for common patterns. LangChain also handles multi-step agentic workflows reasonably well. If your application needs an LLM to decide between tools, loop on results, or execute a sequence of actions based on intermediate outputs, LangChain's agent abstractions give you a starting point without requiring you to build the decision loop yourself. Where It Creates Friction The same breadth that makes LangChain appealing also makes it hard to reason about. The abstraction layers sit deep, and when something breaks, tracing the failure through multiple layers of wrapped classes is non-trivial. Many developers report that LangChain's abstractions initially accelerate development and then create drag during debugging and customization. The framework has also evolved rapidly, which means documentation can lag behind the current API, older tutorials may reference deprecated patterns, and upgrading between versions occasionally introduces breaking changes. For production systems that require stability and predictability, this churn is a real cost. LangChain works best when you're prototyping quickly, exploring what an LLM application could do, or building something where broad integration coverage matters more than tight control over implementation details. LlamaIndex: Focused, Opinionated, Purpose-Built for Retrieval LlamaIndex (formerly GPT Index) started with a narrower scope: making it easier to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. That focus is still its defining characteristic. Where It Works Well If your application is primarily about retrieving information from documents and providing it as context to an LLM, LlamaIndex is exceptionally well-suited. Its data connectors, indexing strategies, and query engines are purpose-built for this use case, and the abstractions are generally more coherent as a result. LlamaIndex also provides solid tooling for more advanced RAG patterns: re-ranking, hybrid search, hierarchical retrieval, and query routing. Teams building production-grade document question-answering systems, knowledge base assistants, or enterprise search applications will find that LlamaIndex handles the edge cases that simpler retrieval pipelines miss. The framework has also invested meaningfully in evaluation tooling, which matters more than it might seem. Knowing whether your retrieval system is actually returning useful context — and knowing that before it affects users — is one of the harder problems in LLM application development. Where It Creates Friction LlamaIndex is less suited to applications that extend beyond retrieval. If you need rich agent behavior, complex tool use, or workflows that don't center on document retrieval, you may find yourself fighting the framework's assumptions rather than working with them. Like LangChain, it also carries abstraction overhead. The more the framework assumes about your architecture, the harder it becomes to deviate from those assumptions when your requirements don't fit the expected pattern. Building From Scratch: More Accessible Than It Sounds "Building from scratch" doesn't mean writing an LLM from scratch. It means calling the model provider's API directly, implementing your own retrieval logic, and building only the abstractions your specific application needs. This approach has become more accessible as the base APIs have matured. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers now offer well-documented APIs with solid client libraries. Vector database providers like Pinecone , Weaviate , and Qdrant have their own SDKs. The infrastructure exists. You're choosing to assemble it yourself rather than through a framework. Where It Works Well Building from scratch gives you complete visibility into what your system is doing at every step. There are no hidden prompt injections from framework templates, no unexpected retry logic, no abstraction layers intercepting your requests. When something behaves unexpectedly, you know exactly where to look. This control becomes especially valuable in production. Teams that have taken LLM applications through the full development lifecycle frequently report that framework constraints become more painful as requirements evolve. Custom retrieval logic, specialized context management, domain-specific prompt engineering, and performance optimization are all easier when you own the implementation. There's also a less obvious benefit: building from scratch forces clarity about what your application actually needs. Frameworks can encourage over-engineering by making complex patterns easy to reach for. When you're implementing retrieval yourself, you'll naturally implement exactly what your use case requires — no more, no less. Where It Creates Friction The upfront investment is real. You'll write more code initially, make more decisions explicitly, and spend more time on infrastructure that frameworks would handle automatically. For teams exploring whether an LLM application is viable at all, that investment may delay learning. There's also a knowledge requirement worth being honest about. Building a good RAG pipeline from scratch requires understanding embedding models, vector similarity, chunking strategies, and context window management. Frameworks can paper over knowledge gaps that scratch-built systems will expose.

title: 7 Checks to Run Before Trusting AI-Generated Code
abstract: 7 Checks to Run Before Trusting AI-Generated Code AI makes writing code cheap. Verifying it is still your job. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on October 19, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence AI coding assistants can generate a large amount of working code in a few minutes. This increases productivity but it also makes them dangerous. Bad AI-generated code does not necessarily look bad. It may compile, pass tests, and use clean variable names while still making the wrong assumption about an API, authorization rule, edge case, or dependency. GitHub warns that AI-generated code can be semantically incorrect and recommends carefully reviewing and testing it before merging. So instead of asking "Does this AI-generated code look good?", run these 7 checks . Does this AI-generated code look good? 1. Inspecting the Diff Before Running Anything Your first check should not be ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude Code, or another model. It should be Git. When coding agents are given access to an entire repository, they sometimes modify more than the task requires. A small bug fix can unexpectedly become a refactor, dependency update, configuration change, and formatting sweep. Start with: git status git diff --stat git diff git diff --stat gives you an immediate picture of the scope. Suppose you asked the agent: Add validation to the email signup endpoint. You expected changes in two files. But the diff says: 12 files changed, 437 insertions(+), 186 deletions(-) Stop there. Before examining whether the code works, ask why the task required hundreds of changed lines. While reviewing the diff, look specifically for: files unrelated to the task deleted tests, disabled validation, and new configuration values permission changes changes to dependency files large refactors hidden inside a feature duplicated helper functions and error handling that ignores failures The goal is simple: make sure the AI solved the task you gave it rather than a larger task it invented. 2. Making the Compiler, Linter, and Type Checker Judge It Humans are terrible compilers. Do not spend ten minutes visually checking syntax that a deterministic tool can check in seconds. For a Python project, your first automated checks might look like: python -m compileall . ruff check . mypy . For JavaScript or TypeScript: npm run lint npx tsc --noEmit npm run build Static type checking is particularly useful with AI-generated code because models can confidently connect values that happen to look compatible but are not. For example: def get_user_id(user: dict[str, str]) -> int: return user["id"] The code looks harmless. But the declared dictionary contains strings while the function claims to return an integer. A type checker can flag this immediately. 3. Verifying Every New Dependency and API This deserves special attention because it is an AI-specific failure mode. Models sometimes invent package names, and those names can look completely plausible. For example, an AI might suggest: pip install fastapi-jwt-auth-plus Do not assume a dependency exists simply because the name sounds reasonable. A 2025 study analyzed 576,000 large language model (LLM)-generated code samples and documented package hallucinations across Python and JavaScript — 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models. This is important because hallucinated package names create an opportunity known as slopsquatting : someone can register a package under a commonly hallucinated name and potentially trick developers into installing it. So whenever AI adds a dependency, verify it independently. For Python: pip index versions package-name For npm: npm view package-name Then check: Does the package actually exist? Is this the official package? Who maintains it? When was it last updated? Does the project genuinely need it? Does the version match the documentation the code appears to use? Did the lockfile suddenly change substantially? Does it introduce known vulnerabilities? Do the same for APIs. If the AI writes: client.responses.stream_async(...) do not assume the method exists because it resembles the rest of an SDK. Open the current official documentation and confirm: class → method → parameters → return type → supported version This is especially important for rapidly changing AI SDKs, cloud APIs, and JavaScript frameworks. Every newly introduced package and every unfamiliar external API should be traceable to an authoritative registry or official documentation. 4. Testing the Behavior, Not the Implementation Now run the existing test suite. For example: pytest -q But a green test suite is only the beginning. The more important question is: What important case is not being tested? Suppose the AI generated: def apply_discount(price, discount): return price - (price * discount / 100) And generated this test: def test_discount(): assert apply_discount(100, 10) == 90 Great. But what about: discount = 0 discount = 100 discount = -10 discount = 150 price = 0 price = None price = "100" AI frequently generates the happy path because the happy path is also what appears most prominently in examples and documentation. For every generated feature, test at least four categories: Normal input Boundary input Invalid input Failure condition For an API endpoint, that might mean: Valid request Missing field Malformed field Unauthorized request Database/service failure Also make sure the AI did not "fix" a failing test by deleting it or weakening the assertion. For critical functions, consider writing the test before showing the implementation to another model . The feature should survive tests for what happens when the user, network, database, file system, and input data do something unexpected. 5. Attacking the Security Boundaries Functional correctness and security are different tests. This function may work: query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'" cursor.execute(query) It may even pass all your unit tests. It is still unsafe. Whenever AI-generated code touches user-controlled input, authentication, databases, files, shell commands, or external URLs, switch from a functional mindset to an adversarial one. Search the patch for areas involving: SQL queries authentication authorization file paths subprocess execution HTML rendering deserialization redirects HTTP requests tokens passwords API keys Ask questions like: Can the user control this string? Can they access somebody else's resource? Can this path escape its intended directory? Can this query be parameterized? Can this command execute arbitrary input? What happens if this URL points to an internal service? Are permissions checked server-side? Then run static security tooling where appropriate. One general-purpose option is Semgrep : semgrep scan --config auto Semgrep documents this configuration for automatically selecting relevant scanning rules. Python projects can also use Bandit : bandit -r . Bandit analyzes Python's abstract syntax tree for common security problems. Repositories using GitHub can enable CodeQL code scanning, which can analyze supported languages on pull requests and protected branches. One more check is important: Search for secrets. Look for: API keys database passwords OAuth tokens private keys cloud credentials connection strings GitHub's secret scanning exists specifically to detect credentials accidentally committed into repositories. An AI assistant should never turn this: api_key = os.environ["API_KEY"] into: api_key = "sk-..." just because it saw a credential in its environment or context. No untrusted input should cross a security boundary without you understanding exactly how it is validated, escaped, authorized, or isolated. 6. Following the Failure Path AI-generated code often looks strong when everything works. So deliberately examine what happens when everything does not work. Consider this generated code: try: response = requests.get(url) return response.

title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
abstract: We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. We split the system into two layers: The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded. One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space: Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability. Each subagent follows a standardized structure: This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first. Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain. When a knowledge file is updated, the next session automatically uses the latest version — no orchestrator changes required. The same knowledge files serve multiple platform implementations of our agent. Configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with our earlier config-driven system. The thin orchestrator system does it in under an hour. For broader context: About two-thirds of the system’s changes land without significant human edits. It gets there by trading generality for deep domain knowledge, a deliberate architectural choice. The orchestrator is general; the subagents are specialists. The conventional approach is to make the orchestrator the smartest component — give it all the context and let it reason about what to do and how to do it. This works until it doesn’t, and it stops working exactly when you need it most — at scale, with complex multi-step workflows, across heterogeneous subsystems. The thin orchestrator works because it aligns architectural boundaries with computational boundaries: This pattern isn’t specific to data pipelines. Any team building production AI agents can benefit: The strongest argument for a thin orchestrator is the failure mode of the alternative. When a heavyweight orchestrator hallucinates, the error spreads to everything downstream: it routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields, or skips reliability checks. A thin orchestrator leaves little room for hallucination because its routing and reliability steps don’t rely on LLM reasoning. It follows a fixed protocol. The creativity happens downstream, in isolated, domain-scoped contexts where hallucination risk is minimized and failures are contained. We’re scaling this architecture to handle an increase in data columns across new pipeline domains. The compositional thesis predicts this will work because scaling means adding workflow templates and knowledge files, not rebuilding agents. We’re also exploring how the system can continuously improve from production usage, using automated feedback loops to identify failure patterns and propose targeted improvements to subagent knowledge, with human review always gating any changes. The counterintuitive lesson: the most important component in our AI agent system is the one that does the least work. Keep your orchestrator thin and your specialists deep, and the whole system becomes more reliable. This work was a team effort. Some other people who contributed to this effort include: Mani Bhushan, Rahul Maliakkal, Jae Ha, Chakrapani Kumar, Vivek Tiwari, and Amanda Yin. The post The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

title: Accelerating Mamba-2 with High-Performance Forward Pass Kernels in NVIDIA CUDA Tile
abstract: NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores. As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them. Overview and prerequisites To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the cuTile Python Quickstart guide. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post. Sequence modeling computational trade-off Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length. Mamba-2 architecture The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores. The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is: \(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\) y t = c t ⊤ h t + D x t y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t Where: \(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\) \(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\) \(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity) \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters Intuitively: \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\) \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply: \(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\) This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores. An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just: \(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\) If building a matrix \(B\) of shape ( T, S ) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape ( T, H ) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\): Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given only \(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula. Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute: \(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\) Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this: Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention). When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection): \(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) With \(M\) the traditional causal mask. Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like: \(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\) Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability. Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe This will translate into three kernels: chunk_cumsum : Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk. fwd_pass_state : Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above. compute_out : Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step. Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk.

title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
abstract: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data. SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases: You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration. From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. This represents a significant expansion of the catalog, driven by the accelerating pace of open source model releases and growing customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes, and capabilities. Here’s a breakdown of the leading contributors and a link to our SageMaker JumpStart page : The models onboarded in 2026 reflect several focused priorities in how we expand the SageMaker JumpStart catalog. These aren’t only industry trends. They represent the areas where we see strong customer demand and significant opportunity to help customers build production AI applications on SageMaker. NVIDIA is one of our significant model providers, and in 2026 their contribution extended well beyond language models. The Cosmos3 world foundation models, available in Super, Edge, and Nano tiers, bring video generation, physics simulation, and action planning into a single architecture for physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and digital twins. Combined with Nemotron models spanning from efficient edge inference (Nano-12B) to large-scale reasoning (Super-120B), SageMaker JumpStart now offers a broad portfolio of NVIDIA open models. If you build on NVIDIA hardware, you can deploy these models on SageMaker with optimized containers and pre-configured endpoints. Customer workloads increasingly require models that process more than text. In 2026, we prioritized onboarding models that handle vision, speech, and document understanding natively. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni processes text, vision, and speech in a single model. Google Gemma 4 adds vision-language capabilities across multiple sizes. IBM granite-speech-4.1-2b handles speech recognition and translation across six languages. Mistral Voxtral-Mini supports real-time speech understanding. These additions mean customers can avoid chaining separate preprocessing models for multimodal workloads. Image and video generation moved from niche to mainstream in 2026. We onboarded FLUX.2 Small Decoder and FLUX.2-klein-base-4B from Black Forest Labs for fast text-to-image generation, Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B for multimodal agentic workflows, and NVIDIA Cosmos3 for video generation. With these models, you can access creative AI capabilities with the same one-click deployment experience you use for language models. Not every workload requires a frontier-scale model, and many customers are focused on optimizing inference costs as they move to production. We onboarded multiple quantized and compact models: Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 FP8 delivers strong performance with a reduced memory footprint. JetBrains Mellum2-12B uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with only 2.5B active parameters for code generation. OpenBMB MiniCPM5-1B packs multimodal capabilities into 1 billion parameters. Microsoft Phi-4-mini-instruct and IBM Granite 4.0 h-tiny demonstrate that compact models serve production workloads on instance types like ml.g5.xlarge. These models can optimize latency and total cost of ownership (TCO) for targeted use cases. General-purpose LLMs are versatile, but purpose-built models are optimized for specific tasks. In 2026, we onboarded Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B for autonomous AI workflows with native tool-calling. GLM-OCR, LightOnOCR, and DeepSeek-OCR handle document text extraction. Qwen3-Reranker-4B and Cohere Rerank v4.0 improve retrieval precision in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. langcache-embed-v3-small provides lightweight embedding for semantic search. Qwen3-ASR and Qwen3-TTS bring speech recognition and synthesis. OpenFold3 supports protein structure prediction for scientific computing. With these models, you can build pipelines where each stage uses the specialized tool for the job, rather than forcing a single model to do everything. Reducing concentration risk in model selection is important for enterprise customers. In 2026, we expanded the catalog to include 30 providers, up from a more concentrated set in prior years. Alibaba Qwen is the single largest contributor with 29 models spanning reasoning, coding, speech, and retrieval. Zhipu AI and DeepSeek add competitive LLMs and specialized OCR. MiniMax and Moonshot AI contribute emerging architectures. Cohere brings reliable reranking. BharatGenAI and Kakao expand regional model coverage. This breadth gives customers more options for performance, cost, licensing, and language support. Beyond model onboarding, SageMaker JumpStart also shipped significant improvements in 2026 that reduce friction across the model lifecycle, from discovery to deployment. Previously, discovering SageMaker JumpStart models required navigating into SageMaker Studio and finding the SageMaker JumpStart section in the left navigation. The new Model Hub experience surfaces the full SageMaker JumpStart catalog directly on the SageMaker AI console landing page. You can browse models by category and filter by input/output modality, publisher, model size, license, and framework. You can also view sample notebooks and open models inside Studio with a single click. This avoids the multi-step navigation that slowed initial exploration. Choosing the right instance type, serving container, and optimization settings for a model deployment typically required manual benchmarking across dozens of combinations. SageMaker JumpStart now offers named deployment configurations, with optimization options for: These configurations include Neuron-optimized setups for AWS Inferentia and AWS Trainium instances, reducing deployment complexity and infrastructure costs. You can deploy a model with a single click and the right optimization profile, rather than spending weeks benchmarking configurations manually. A new integration with Hugging Face connects model discovery directly to SageMaker Studio, for onboarded models. When browsing models on Hugging Face, you can choose Deploy on SageMaker AI or Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI . You land directly in a configured Studio environment with the model pre-loaded, permissions pre-configured, and GPU quota visibility built in. This avoids the need to set up AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, create a domain, or configure permissions before experimenting. There are three ways to get started with SageMaker JumpStart: Each model on SageMaker JumpStart includes deployment configurations, sample notebooks, and documentation. For a hands-on walkthrough, see our related blog post on “ Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart ”. title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
abstract: On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock . Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON. Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains. With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing. With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary. In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting. Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions: Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including: Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated. Each request runs in one of two analysis modes, chosen with the analysisMode field: You can point the model at video in two ways. An S3 location ( s3Location ) takes the object’s uri and the bucketOwner account ID, and suits long-form video. A base64 string ( base64String ) embeds the video in the request body, up to 25 MB, and suits short clips. To track cost by application, create an application inference profile from the Pegasus 1.5 model, tag it, and call it by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in place of the model ID. The following section outlines how to get started with Pegasus 1.5. Before you begin, make sure you have: The following policy grants both invoke actions on Pegasus 1.5. Boto3 signs requests with your usual AWS credentials. You can also authenticate with an Amazon Bedrock API key by setting it in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable. For production, prefer a short-term key generated from your IAM credentials with the aws-bedrock-token-generator package, because it expires automatically. Bearer-token authentication also requires the bedrock:CallWithBearerToken permission. The following example analyzes a video stored in Amazon S3 in general mode. This example uses the global Cross Region Inference (CRIS) endpoint. To target the US geographic endpoint instead, replace “global.” with “us.” in the endpoint URL. The response carries the answer in message , the token counts in input_tokens and output_tokens , and the reason generation ended in stopReason . A stopReason of length means the answer reached maxOutputTokens before it finished, so check it before you rely on the output: Request fields for general mode: For a short clip, you can send the video inline instead of from S3: Note that the preceding example uses the optional includeMetering attribute. includeMetering: True makes Pegasus 1.5 add two billing-usage fields to the non-streaming response: outputTokenCount and inputVideoSecond (the analyzed video’s duration in seconds). For interactive applications, InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the answer in chunks as it’s generated. Each chunk carries the next piece of text in message : In general mode, you can constrain the answer to a JSON Schema so downstream code can parse it directly. Set responseFormat.type to json_schema and put the schema under jsonSchema . The answer arrives in message as a JSON string: Time-based metadata generation is where Pegasus 1.5 differs most from earlier versions. Instead of a prompt, you send one or more segment definitions, and the model returns every segment of the video that matches each one. Set analysisMode to time_based_metadata and responseFormat.type to segment_definitions . The definitions take the place of inputPrompt , so leave that field out. Each definition has: The following example identifies each editorial section in a news broadcast and returns a title, summary, and key topics for each one: The previous sample code when tested against a sports clip may produce an output like the following sample. Each segment carries start_sec , end_sec , and the fields you defined. segmentTimeFormat controls how the times are written: seconds returns numbers you can do arithmetic on, while hh:mm:ss and hh:mm:ss.fff return readable timestamps as strings. The response also includes a definition_errors list, which is empty when every definition was processed. A single request can include multiple segment definitions, for example one for editorial sections and another for on-screen brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns the matches for all of them in one segments list, and tags each segment with _definition_id so you can tell them apart. The following example adds a second definition to the previous request and groups the results: Because the schema is defined once, the same definitions can be applied across an entire video library, producing consistent metadata for every asset. Pegasus 1.5 introduces multimodal prompting, so you can include reference images alongside your text prompts. This is useful when you want to ask the model about specific objects, people, or scenes that are easier to show than describe. For example, you can provide a product image and ask the model to identify every moment where that product appears in a video. Or you can provide a reference image of a specific logo and ask the model to detect brand appearances and their timestamps. This capability enhances the precision of video analysis, and opens up use cases such as visual brand monitoring, product placement analysis, and image-guided content search. Reference images attach differently depending on the mode. In general mode, put them in promptV2.mediaSources , alongside the question in promptV2.inputText . In segmentation mode ( analysisMode: time_based_metadata ), attach them to the mediaSources of each segment definition inside responseFormat.segmentDefinitions . A definition can then match a visual reference as well as a text description. Each image needs a name , a media_type of image , and exactly one source: either an inline base64String or an s3Location with uri and bucketOwner . A single request can carry up to 30 reference images. A general-mode request asks the model about an object shown in a reference image.
