Use them to track volume and latency. Pair them with application inference profiles when you need usage broken down by application. Pegasus 1.5 is designed for organizations that manage large volumes of long-form video: In each case, people remain part of the workflow. Their work shifts from finding and tagging every moment by hand to reviewing and refining the metadata generated by the model.

title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
abstract: As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI. For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability. In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription. Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile . We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile . The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected. We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile . Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target. From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution. We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size. Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills. In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels. Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica. Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API ( libnrt ). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size. We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline. Figure 1: Deepgram Nova-3 on AWS Trainium2, compiled ahead of time and served from Rust We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads. To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation , which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from.

title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
abstract: vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT). One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline. Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration. We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path. Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons: The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance. The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together. Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate The protocol has three logical steps. 1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill. 2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests. 3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode. The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution. The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request. Figure 3: Main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request in the push-based threading model The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner. Figure 4: Pull and push transfer flows compared, highlighting how push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.

title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
abstract: Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT). When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow. In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA ), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes. We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router. We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions. The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix. Figure 1: Standard prefill-to-decode flow (blue) and the bi-directional KV transfer additions (red) vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment. The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params . The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node. The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the conversation_id so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn. Figure 2: KV-cache-aware router metadata flow across conversation turns Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime ( decoder_kv_blocks_ttl , default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer. KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The kv_recompute_threshold setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance. For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B and GLM-5-FP8 models on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA.

title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later. My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves. Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world – as we’ve heard in so many sessions here – and is contributing to its own development. Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work. What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why. For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up. They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun. The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities — on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” The singularity is here . The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril. Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development. I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly – ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find. But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. As a consequence, the field of software development is changing – A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans. We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life. But new AI capabilities bring new challenges – the coding improvements have meant AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these powerful capabilities to create better cyberdefenses, while bad actors race to use these systems to carry out hacks. The important thing to notice here is that these things are bound up, inseparably – the advance of AI systems in a general area like coding has also created both positive and negative impacts in domains of international relevance, like cybersecurity. This is a taste of things to come. Of progress yielding new capabilities, and new challenges. These capabilities will not stop at coding; the same thing will happen to science and robotics. It has already begun to happen. And it means some important properties of the global economy may change – like the rate of innovation, or the frequency with which we invent entirely new general purpose technologies that create new industries around themselves, like the internet, phones, and artificial intelligence. So, what causes me to believe this? In 2026, we have got the first signs that AI systems may be capable of doing science at the frontier, and we have some evocative examples of what the future could look like. For instance: In mathematics, AI systems have been used to propose solutions to longstanding mathematical problems, like the Navier Stokes Millenium Prize, the Jacobian Conjecture, and several open Erdos problems. In many cases, AI systems were responsible for core insights that made the solution possible. In biology, researchers have used AI to design viruses from scratch, to identify new drug candidates for testing, and there are already drugs in trials today which have been in large part designed by AI. In robotics, AI systems are now increasingly able to autonomously operate laboratory equipment remotely, making it possible for us to further automate experimentation in domains from biology to materials science, making progress faster in areas like batteries and fuel-cell development. Taken individually, each of these examples is exciting.

title: VAST開源即時世界模型EdenLive！單消費級顯示卡、720P超24FPS
abstract: VAST開源即時世界模型EdenLive！單消費級顯示卡、720P超24FPS 聽雨 2026-10-18 19:49:49 來源： 量子位 讓人人都能自由創造並體驗可互動世界 聽雨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI VAST的世界模型，今天有了新成果。 即時世界模型 EdenLive ，正式釋出並開源。 據VAST介紹，EdenLive首次實現了在即時生成的前提下，同時完成任意參考輸入、任意畫風生成和長時連續執行。 具體來說，給它簡化場景或參考影片，再配上目標首幀和提示詞，就能沿著參考的佈局與運動，持續生成寫實、二次元等不同畫風的精細畫面。 參考來源可以不同，生成畫風可以指定，而這些變化都能在即時生成過程中呈現。 在單張消費級顯示卡Nvidia RTX 5090上、720P條件下，5B模型的生成速度 超過24FPS ，還能持續生成分鐘級畫面。 據VAST介紹，從使用者輸入操作到對應畫面出現，這套系統目前的端到端延遲為百毫秒級。 畫面持續變化的同時，互動規則和世界狀態由上游互動系統維護。系統接收玩家操作、更新狀態，EdenLive再根據對應的參考畫面，將這些變化即時呈現出來。 最近，AI在3D場景搭建與互動創作上的能力，變得越來越直觀。 GPT-6 Astra 就是一個典型例子：它已經能夠在Blender裡搭建房屋，再將其轉入Unreal Engine 5，形成可以進入、漫遊的場景。 當AI能夠搭建場景、設計互動玩法，如何讓這些內容獲得精細且即時的視覺表現，也就成為接下來需要解決的問題。 在這樣的背景下，一條技術路線逐漸成為行業共識： 由互動系統維護底層狀態和執行規則，再由生成模型負責視覺渲染 。 而這套分工，VAST早在今年6月初就已經明確並對外發布成果。 當時公開的Project Eden研究預覽，已將 「狀態維護與視覺渲染解耦」 作為核心設計。 從時間上看，這一路線選擇早於行業共識形成約3-4個月。 如今，EdenLive作為這條路線的階段性成果釋出，並開放模型權重和推理程式碼，同步公開技術報告與端到端Demo。 程式碼： https://github.com/VAST-AI-Research/EdenLive 專案主頁： https://vast-eden.ai/?p=edenlive 技術報告： https://assets.vast-eden.ai/assets/edenlive/EdenLive-tech-report.pdf 開放權重： https://huggingface.co/VAST-AI/EdenLive 多種參考輸入，不同畫風即時生成 EdenLive的核心價值，在於為簡化場景和互動內容提供高質量即時渲染，底層邏輯與狀態則繼續由上游互動系統維護。 它具體能做什麼？我們先來欣賞一波Demo。 互動式遊戲預覽 首先是互動式遊戲預覽，2D、3D場景都可以接入。 現階段，EdenLive更適合場景漫遊、推箱子等互動相對低頻的玩法，讓創作者在操作遊戲原型的同時，檢視精細畫面下的呈現效果。 【此處無法插入影片，遺憾……可到量子位公眾號檢視～】 比如岩漿闖關，角色用冷凍槍製造落腳點，再通過跳躍一路前進。 要讓這樣的遊戲畫面隨著操作持續更新，生成速度首先得跟上。 據VAST公佈的資料，在單張消費級顯示卡RTX 5090、720P條件下，EdenLive的5B模型生成速度 超過24FPS ，也就是每秒生成超過24幀畫面。 另一個Demo——雙人對打遊戲，則能具體展示角色動作與血條、回合計時等遊戲狀態的配合。 除了畫面更新速度，按下按鍵後多久能看到反饋，也直接影響互動體驗。 據VAST介紹，EdenLive目前從使用者輸入到對應畫面出現，端到端延遲為百毫秒級。 這套系統還支援分鐘級連續生成，讓場景漫遊和連續操作有更長的展開空間。 場景與動畫預覽 除了遊戲互動，EdenLive還可以用於場景與動畫預覽，在場景佈局和運鏡已經確定的基礎上，更換不同的美術風格。 比如，讓大家天天玩的「鵜鶘騎腳踏車」成真…… 從未見過如此栩栩如生之鵜鶘啊。 生成畫面不僅讓羽毛和海邊環境有了細緻的質感，還模擬出了真實的光影。 用簡單模型搭出的雪地行車場景，經EdenLive生成後，也呈現出了更寫實的車身紋理、積雪和光影效果。 這些畫面的生成，由三類輸入共同控制：參考畫面提供場景佈局、鏡頭與運動，目標首幀設定整體外觀和畫風，提示詞則補充風格與細節。 因此，同一套佈局和運鏡，可以用來生成不同美術風格的版本，供導演和概念設計師比較、選擇。 影片重渲染與換⽪ 已有影片也可以交給EdenLive重新渲染，即時替換角色形象、畫面內容和整體風格。 比如，將藍色背景前的真人轉換成卡通角色，但人物姿態和服裝配色仍與參考畫面保持一致。 這類用法類似虛擬主播換形象，以真人的動作作為參考，生成另一種角色外觀。 再比如，將實拍房屋轉換成手繪動畫風格。 房屋的大體佈局得到保留，屋頂、牆面和窗框則用線條重新勾勒，色彩與光影也變得更加柔和。 具⾝資料增強 EdenLive還可以用於具身資料增強，將真實人類操作畫面轉成機器人視角，並對第一視角影片中的物體和外觀進行修改。 比如這段影片中，人手拿著噴壺和抹布清潔檯面。 經EdenLive生成後，雙手被替換成機械手，抹布從橙色變成了黃色，但清潔動作仍然與原影片保持一致。 除了替換操作主體，第一視角影片中的物體、材質和顏色也可以調整。 比如把人手替換成金屬機械手臂，推車扶手換成銀色金屬質感，但抓握和推行的動作與原影片保持一致。 這樣，已有操作影片就能衍生出不同外觀的版本，為具身研究擴展影片樣本。 從簡單的2D動畫、3D場景，到實拍影片和第一視角操作畫面，這些不同來源的素材，都可以作為EdenLive的參考輸入。 用同一模型接收多種參考，沿著已有佈局與運動改變視覺表現，再以即時、分鐘級連續生成的方式輸出畫面，正是這組Demo共同展示的核心能力。 現階段，EdenLive也仍存在一些需要改善的地方。 高頻、激烈的互動對生成速度和動作呈現有更高要求；多個角色同時出現時的身份保持、小物體的精細控制，以及長時間生成中的視覺一致性，也有進一步提升的空間。 不過，VAST已經開放了不同規格的模型權重和推理程式碼，同時公開了技術報告和上述端到端Demo。 官方還將同步開源 Game Prototype Turbo ，一款「Prompt to Proxy Game」Skill。 使用者可以通過它快速生成可直接遊玩的遊戲原型。遊戲執行時，互動系統持續更新狀態，並輸出對應的簡化參考畫面；EdenLive再將這些畫面即時渲染為精細的視覺內容，反饋給玩家，形成從遊戲邏輯到即時視覺呈現的完整鏈路。 大家都可以去體驗一下～ 拆解EdenLive技術路線與核心壁壘 接下來，我們來看看EdenLive背後的技術路線究竟是怎樣的。 其採用的核心技術是 「解耦世界狀態與視覺渲染」 ，也就是把世界如何執行、畫面如何呈現分開處理。 比如這段街頭對打Demo： 角色的移動、攻擊和防禦，都由玩家按下相應按鍵來控制；互動系統接收操作，更新角色位置和動作，並判斷攻擊是否命中、血量如何變化。 EdenLive則根據這些變化生成畫面，讓左邊簡單的方塊角色，在右邊呈現為更寫實的人物。 玩家看到畫面反饋，再繼續按鍵操作，遊戲便沿著這套迴圈推進。 我們把這套分工放進完整管線，還能看得更直觀： 圖中，簡化場景或參考影片提供佈局與運動，目標首幀和提示詞指定外觀與細節。 EdenLive結合這些輸入，持續輸出精細畫面；遊戲邏輯和狀態更新，則由上游互動系統負責。 這也呈現出了EdenLive在Project Eden中的職責。 Project Eden 是VAST長期推進的世界模型研究專案，EdenLive則是其中聚焦即時生成式渲染的階段性成果。 管線看起來清楚，但實際做起來，還需要同時兼顧幾件事： 畫面足夠精細、動作跟得上參考、生成速度滿足互動需求，還能持續執行。 這就涉及資料如何採集和配對，以及3D、影片生成與系統工程之間如何協作。 首先是 資料積累 。 要讓模型把簡單的方塊角色生成寫實人物，同時與參考畫面保持相應動作，就需要建立參考與生成畫面之間的對應關係。 場景佈局、鏡頭運動和物體位置，都需要在資料中得到對齊。 據VAST介紹，其資料管線覆蓋2D、3D簡化場景、引擎渲染和真實影片等多種來源的成對資料。 從素材採集、場景構建到資料配對，這些工作共同支撐了EdenLive對不同參考和場景的處理能力。 第二層積累，來自 跨領域的團隊協作 。 EdenLive涉及3D、影片生成與系統工程：既要處理空間結構和運動約束，也要生成細緻的視覺效果，還要讓模型以足夠快的速度持續執行。 而VAST的團隊配置，也覆蓋了這幾個方向。 這些要求需要放在同一套系統裡協調。畫面質量提高後，推理速度能否跟上；外觀發生變化時，角色動作能否繼續貼合參考，都需要模型與工程團隊共同解決。 第三層積累，則是 路線判斷與持續研發 。 在此前公開的Project Eden研究預覽中，VAST已經明確提出 「解耦」 設計： 將世界狀態與視覺生成分離，讓底層狀態獨立於攝像機視角持續存在，再由渲染模組將其呈現為畫面。 圍繞這一思路，VAST進一步給出了三層架構：持續演化的結構化狀態、狀態到觀測的介面，以及生成式神經渲染，分別承擔狀態維護、觀測轉換和畫面生成的職責。 這一路線選擇比行業共識提前了約三四個月。這段時間，也構成了團隊沿著既定方向繼續積累資料、打磨模型與系統的研發視窗。 沿著3D這條路，走向可互動的世界 從這套分工來看， EdenLive延續的仍然是VAST原有的路線 。 構建一個可互動的世界，需要角色、道具和場景資產，也需要明確物體的位置、尺度與空間關係。3D為這些內容提供了可組織、可操作的基礎，並參與世界狀態的表達。 影片生成則負責細緻的視覺呈現，將已有的結構與運動轉化為豐富的材質、光影和動態效果。 兩者結合，才能讓創作者一邊調整場景和玩法，一邊獲得相應的畫面。 這也解釋了，VAST為什麼會進一步走向世界模型研究。 原有3D模型的能力，除了生成資產，還可以參與構建世界模型所需的資料。 在Project Eden的研究介紹中，VAST提到，團隊利用已有3D能力，從影片中提取深度、相機位姿和幾何運動軌跡等結構資訊；同時，利用遊戲引擎獲取相互對應的狀態資訊與渲染畫面。 這些工作，將VAST此前在3D模型和資料管線上的積累，延伸到了世界模型需要解決的結構、狀態與視覺對應問題上。 從創作流程看，這條路線也在逐步擴大使用者能夠完成的事情：生成角色和道具，搭建場景，加入互動規則，再為執行中的內容賦予不同的視覺表現。 這也對應著VAST提出的願景： 讓人人都能自由創造並體驗可互動世界 。 Project Eden承擔著這一長期探索，EdenLive則先推進其中的即時生成式渲染環節。 對於創作者，它也提供了一個更具體的入口：把已經能執行的場景和玩法接入模型，在實際操作中嘗試畫面效果，在此基礎上繼續修改自己的作品。 One More Thing 等等，先別划走。 如果你感興趣的話，VAST也在為這些研究尋找新同事。 其推出的 V·STAR頂尖人才計劃 ，全年開放招聘，面向全球青年演算法與研究人才，聚焦3D生成基礎模型、三維理解、智慧體與世界模型。 VAST強調開放、扁平的研究環境，鼓勵年輕研究者提出新想法，好的技術思路可以快速立項、驗證，即便是實習生，也有機會參與核心模型訓練，深入模型研發與工程實踐。 待遇也是真的香～ 無論是全職還是實習生都有機會拿到比頭部大廠更具競爭力的薪資，特別優秀者上不封頂，還有長期期權。 如果你也想擁有定義問題的自由，從零推動一個專案，親歷一家頭部AI公司從1到100的爆發式成長，獲得最寶貴的創業經驗，可以試試這個投遞通道： 簡歷傳送至vstar.talent@vastai3d.com，郵件標題請註明：VSTAR – 姓名 – 畢業時間 — 完 — 量子位 QbitAI · 頭條號簽約 關注我們，第一時間獲知前沿科技動態 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 聽雨 title: Together Post-Training: frontier-grade model shaping, the way that fits you
abstract: We are introducing Together Post-Training, a new service for building custom models on our platform — both from environment rewards via RL and supervision data via SFT. This service is designed to give you flexible and efficient model shaping without the heavy infra burden. Together Post-Training makes it easy to define the training loop, while we co-optimize the systems and infrastructure underneath for model quality and training speed. Nothing now stands between you and the best model that is uniquely yours . The value of custom models In 2026, training custom models for your AI workloads is no longer a niche topic. Companies are actively exploring it to reduce costs and improve task-specific performance. Instead of fixing model behaviors and improving their efficiency via context or harness engineering, many AI-native and AI-forward organizations are training specialist agents, matching the quality of frontier models at a fraction of the cost and runtime. On top of that, training the model yourself yields greater ownership and flexibility: the resulting checkpoint can be deployed in any location, further refined, or even used locally. At Together, we want to empower every AI developer with the ability to get the best model for their task, as conveniently as possible. Post-training a great model requires many iterations on data curation, training algorithms, and evaluation protocols. On top of that, infrastructure for RL is getting ever more complex, with a fine line between “an efficiency optimization” and “a silent bug that holds back your runs”. Doing so for large models reliably and at scale presents its own set of challenges. Frontier labs have entire teams solving each of the above problems. Since tackling all challenges at once is a big investment, many companies that could benefit from post-training never start it, or start and stall. Together Post-Training handles all optimizations and infrastructure without getting in the way, and our forward-deployed team partners with our customers to help with the end-to-end workflow. This lets every researcher or domain expert focus on what they do best while we take care of the rest. Together Post-Training at a glance As the complexity of post-training continues to evolve, so should the tooling around it. Together Post-Training provides a set of common abstractions familiar to ML developers, as well as control over the resources used by each experiment, while making sure that all computations under the hood are fast, cost-efficient, and, most importantly, correct. We built our service to offer the highest degree of flexibility for your experiments. You can run LoRA training, including multiple LoRA adapters sharing the same GPU capacity, as well as full-weight experiments for select models. In contrast to our fine-tuning service , the entire training loop of Together Post-Training is yours to define. You can use any data, environments, or agentic harnesses that suit your setup best, and add any steps you need (such as logging or external benchmarking) throughout the training process. The entire workflow is as follows: A high-level summary of using Together Post-Training. Left: commands executed on the user side, right: service components running on Together’s side. All experiments run on Model Resources — GPU allocations that are fully yours, not competing with others’ requests for priority. Each Model Resource can hold one or several Training Sessions, where each one corresponds to a single experiment using the same base model (for example, one set of LoRA adapters). This means you get the best rollout and training performance, as you never have to compete with other users’ requests executing on the same hardware. At the same time, dedicated GPU allocations mean you can run full-weight finetuning, going beyond LoRA when adapting to large knowledge-intensive tasks. Once you allocate the model resource and start the session, you can execute each step of the training loop. Each session contains a Trainer instance responsible for running forward/backward steps and updating the weights, as well as Generator instances for executing rollouts from the policy. For every model, we heavily optimize training and rollout performance, making sure all operations are fast and numerically aligned across stacks. In the case of SFT, you can start a model resource with 0 generators to save costs. You decide the point at which the trainer parameters are sent to the generator; we also support asynchronous RL for high GPU utilization of both components at all times, especially with long agentic rollouts. While we support a number of standard losses (from cross-entropy and GRPO to CISPO and DPPO), we also allow computing a custom training objective locally and sending its gradients to the Trainer for computing the updates. Example of training with a custom loss from Together Post-Training docs Together Post-Training launches with a range of leading open-weight models, including Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8-27B. We will expand the selection in the coming weeks, making sure you can use both the highest-capability frontier LLMs and efficient smaller models. Quality, performance, and efficiency Delegating the internals of post-training infrastructure can be a daunting decision. Our team has first-hand experience catching silent bugs in complex machine learning systems, from pushing the frontier of RL research to training LLMs that have served millions of users. We understand that the best training stack is the one that gets you the best model , and building such infrastructure demands careful implementation and co-design across all components. For these reasons, we prioritized quality of output models as our north star in the development of the service. One notorious example of issues affecting RL results is the alignment between training and inference engines: if the same model weights produce slightly different outputs due to mismatching numerics, the whole run might underperform or even collapse. We eliminate numerous sources of policy drift across training and inference, using both standard techniques like Rollout Routing Replay and advanced optimizations driven by our research in training stability. Beyond model quality, we also work to make each run as fast and as efficient as possible, because post-training requires multiple iterations: the sooner a run finishes and the less it costs, the more ideas you get to test. Most of the time in RL is spent on generating rollouts, which allows us to capitalize on years of research and engineering behind Together’s inference products. Our rollout engines draw on the same optimizations as our serving stack. For multi-turn agents, intelligent caching and routing minimize redundant computations while keeping memory costs bounded. On the training side, optimized parallelism and sequence packing speed up both SFT and RL steps. With Together Post-Training, you size each experiment to what it needs and do not pay more. If your experiment is bottlenecked by rollout concurrency, you can request the exact number of sampler replicas. Several LoRA experiments can share one model resource, so running a sweep doesn’t mean reserving more GPUs for every setup. We bill every model resource per GPU-minute, yet thanks to many optimizations of our dedicated and multi-LoRA serving stacks, the overall costs of training drop below token-based pricing as soon as you scale up the experiments. Optimized deployment after training When the post-training experiments are finished, it might be important to run each resulting model side by side to compare their outputs. We now support multi-LoRA adapter serving in Dedicated Model Inference: instead of starting a separate production deployment for each run, you can swap the adapters at your convenience in a single GPU deployment, helping you lower the serving costs.

title: What makes a catalog open? Unity Catalog Advances the Open Lakehouse
abstract: While almost every platform now supports open formats, what makes a catalog truly open? An open catalog keeps your data in storage you own , gives you the best features there, and supports data portability : the ability to move your tables to another catalog while keeping the data in place . Portability is a core tenet of an open lakehouse, and it’s where most catalogs fall short. As the first catalog to support both REGISTER and UNREGISTER from the Apache Iceberg™ REST catalog spec, Unity Catalog in Databricks' Open Lakehouse expands what an open catalog means: your tables can move existing Iceberg tables in or out without any data movement. Databricks contributed UNREGISTER to the Iceberg REST catalog spec, making this an open standard. Read Unlocking Data Portability . This post walks through the three requirements of an open catalog, how Unity Catalog meets each one, and compares what happens to the same Iceberg table on different platforms. How open a lakehouse is comes down to the catalog. Many providers still use a proprietary format for the primary table type in their catalog, so formats are important to pay attention to. Beyond this however, an open catalog must also meet three requirements: Teams move tables into provider-controlled storage to get features the customer-owned option lacks. From then on, the provider's roadmap decides what you can do with your data. Changing catalogs means exporting and rewriting every table, to move it out of provider-controlled storage. Most data platforms support open table formats like Apache Iceberg. However, when those tables live in buckets that belong to the provider, your tables are no longer open. That makes the format open in name only: you can't see the files in your own cloud account, storage is billed through the provider, and leaving means copying every table out first. Unity Catalog takes the opposite approach. In Databricks, "managed" describes who maintains a table, not who owns its storage. The catalog handles optimization, maintenance, and upgrades, while the files stay in a cloud storage account you own, not in the proprietary storage other platforms often call "managed storage." In Databricks, 99% of UC managed tables are in customer-owned storage. On platforms built around provider-controlled storage, it’s the opposite: nearly all of their tables live in storage that the provider controls and are locked in a proprietary format by default. The difference shows up the day you decide to leave a catalog. Owning your storage only matters if the catalog treats those tables as first-class. Some platforms offer a customer-owned storage option, but reserve their best capabilities for tables in managed storage they control, creating an illusion of openness. The open path exists, but it comes with fewer features, so most tables would end up in provider managed storage anyway. With Unity Catalog managed tables, the best features are supported for customer-owned storage (“bring your own storage”) path, whereas other platforms have limitations: The most important test for whether a catalog is open is portability: whether you can leave the catalog easily at any time by moving tables between catalogs without having to copy out data. Until recently, the ecosystem didn’t have a standard way to release a table from a catalog's management. Therefore, Databricks contributed UNREGISTER to the Apache Iceberg REST catalog specification which gives customers the freedom to leave without having to copy, move or rewrite any data files. In Unity Catalog, REGISTER and UNREGISTER work as a pair: This is made possible because Unity Catalog managed tables reside in storage that you own. Unregistering isn’t possible with provider controlled storage since the exit API can’t hand you a pointer to files that you can't take with you. Unity Catalog managed tables are fully portable and open with no lock-in: you retain control of your own data. To get started in Databricks, reach out to your account team to get access to REGISTER and UNREGISTER (in Private Preview). With REGISTER and UNREGISTER, your Iceberg tables move to Unity Catalog with zero data copy into Databricks, stay fully open in your own storage, and gain all the benefits of Unity Catalog and Predictive Optimization: To learn more, read Unlocking Data Portability . See Unity Catalog managed tables documentation for more details on how to use Unity Catalog managed tables, which exist in customer-owned storage. In the future, we plan to support converting foreign tables or external tables to Databricks to managed tables using SET MANAGED IN PLACE. This would allow you to keep the same customer-defined storage path as before and does not require any data movement. Yes. Unity Catalog is open source and meets three requirements of an open catalog. Its managed tables, in Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake, live in a cloud storage account you own, get the full feature set there, and can move to another catalog without copying data through REGISTER and UNREGISTER. Most importantly, Unity Catalog managed tables are in customer-owned storage, so UNREGISTER in Databricks provides catalog portability without data movement on the Unity Catalog side. Read and write access to manage tables is also supported, using Unity Catalog and Iceberg REST Catalog Open APIs. Not on its own. An Iceberg table in provider-controlled storage can be as hard to move as a proprietary table, and an Iceberg table in your own storage may get fewer features. Avoiding lock-in also requires storage you own, full features on those tables, and a catalog that supports a clean, no-copy handoff. In Unity Catalog, "managed" describes who maintains a table, not who owns its storage. Unity Catalog managed tables are optimized and maintained by the catalog, and their files live in a cloud storage account you own. On some other platforms, "managed storage" means storage the provider owns and controls, not just optimizes. Yes. With UNREGISTER, you can remove a table from Unity Catalog and register it in another Iceberg REST catalog, without copying data files. In Unity Catalog, "managed" describes who maintains a table, not who owns its storage. Unity Catalog managed tables are optimized and maintained by the catalog, but their files live in a cloud storage account you own. On some other platforms, "managed storage" means storage the provider owns and often keeps in proprietary table formats. Foreign Iceberg tables are read-only in Databricks because another catalog owns their commits, which prevents two catalogs from writing to the same table. To have Unity Catalog manage the table in customer-owned storage, register it in Unity Catalog with REGISTER. You can also convert foreign tables to Unity Catalog managed tables in customer-owned storage using SET MANAGED. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: New course teaches how AI models run on modern accelerators
abstract: Most engineers building AI models today work on GPUs. They write models in PyTorch, run them, and measure latency and utilization. What happens between the framework and the silicon often remains hidden. That was manageable when one architecture dominated. It is much harder now, as AI hardware has diversified across GPUs, Google TPUs, the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE), the Groq Language Processing Unit (LPU), and IBM's Spyre accelerator. A new Coursera specialization, Dataflow Architectures for AI: From Principles to Practice , is built for engineers who need to work across that range. Taught by Kaoutar El Maghraoui, a principal research scientist at IBM Research and adjunct professor of computer science at Columbia University, the six-course program covers execution models, compilation, memory systems, debugging, and performance modeling through hands-on labs. "Sometimes the model itself isn't the difficult part," said El Maghraoui. "The difficult part is understanding how that model maps onto a particular architecture and why something that works very well on one system may behave completely differently on another." One PyTorch model and five execution models The specialization starts from a single PyTorch model. At the framework level it is the same nn.Module on every target. Once a compiler maps it onto hardware, the execution looks very different, and each stack supports its own set of operators, layouts, and graph transformations. A GPU runs the model as kernels across many parallel threads, with hardware-managed caches and specialized matrix units. A TPU maps the work onto systolic arrays, with the XLA compiler directing tiling and data movement. Cerebras spreads compute and more than 40 GB of on-chip SRAM across a full wafer. Groq relies on its compiler to schedule when each operation runs and when data moves. Spyre compiles the model into a dataflow graph, and its compiler decides layout and scratchpad placement while the runtime orchestrates transfers and launches. The details vary by product generation. Those choices change which optimizations matter. Fusion removes intermediate memory traffic, but how much it saves depends on whether the compiler already keeps intermediates on chip, how tensors are tiled, and whether the fused kernel adds memory pressure. A tensor dimension that maps cleanly on one target can require padding or data rearrangement on another. The specialization treats dataflow execution as an architectural class with shared principles. Each concept is introduced in general terms before any specific system is discussed. Spyre is the main worked example because El Maghraoui's team works with it directly, but it is one of five systems compared throughout. Two implementations of the same operation can also run at very different speeds for reasons that have little to do with arithmetic. For matrix multiplication and attention, tiling, data layout, synchronization, and movement between on-chip and off-chip memory often set the achievable performance. Figure 1: The Accelerator Landscape Map. Students carry this table through all six courses and add the reasoning behind each cell as they go. "There's no single architecture that wins every row," El Maghraoui said. "GPUs prioritize flexibility and broad programmability. Other systems give up some of that flexibility in order to gain efficiency, determinism, scale, or tighter control over execution." The compiler gets particular attention. On specialized accelerators it is responsible for tiling, fusion, scheduling, placement, and memory management. That is where much of the performance is won or lost during model enablement. "You can have an accelerator that's extremely efficient for the operations it supports," she said, "but then one unsupported operator, one tensor shape that maps badly, or one memory-placement problem can have a large impact on the full model." Figure 2: A simplified view of PyTorch compilation, covered in Course 3. Which transformations run depends on the compilation mode and the backend. With torch.compile, Inductor does the lowering by default, and torch-spyre extends it for Spyre. TPUs lower through XLA instead. Dataflow backends make most of their fusion, tiling, and placement decisions during lowering. What the specialization covers The specialization is a sequence of six courses. Each course covers one layer of the stack, and each ends in a lab. Together they build up the accelerator landscape map one row at a time. Completing all six earns the professional certificate in AI Systems Performance Engineering. Course 1 — The accelerator landscape : Domain-specific architectures, control-flow and dataflow execution, memory hierarchies, and programming models across all five systems. Course 2 — Dataflow execution models : Nodes, edges, firing rules, and static and dynamic scheduling. A transformer attention block traced through Spyre and TPU. Course 3 — Compilation for dataflow : TorchDynamo, AOTAutograd, and backend code generation. Fusion, tiling, and scheduling in XLA and the Spyre compiler. Course 4 — Memory systems : Caches, scratchpads, and SRAM-only designs. How each memory hierarchy changes KV cache management for LLM inference. Course 5 — Debugging across the dataflow stack : An eight-layer taxonomy of failures, including graph capture errors and scheduling deadlocks, DMA timeouts, and numerical issues. Course 6 — Performance modeling and optimization : Roofline analysis adapted for software-managed memory, with scheduling measured as a third bottleneck alongside compute and memory. Debugging and performance across the stack On a dataflow accelerator, a wrong result or a slowdown often shows up far from its cause. A NaN at the model output can come from an operator decomposition, a fusion pass, a tensor layout mismatch, or a DMA error. Course 5 organizes these failures into an eight-layer taxonomy, from graph capture errors in the frontend to scheduling conflicts, deadlocks, DMA timeouts, and numerical issues in the backend. For correctness, students shrink the failure to a small reproducer, compare each layer's output against a CPU or GPU reference, and find the first point where results diverge. For performance, Course 6 bounds the timed region, splits kernel time from transfer time, compares the result against the compiler's ideal, and attributes the remainder to bytes moved at each memory level. Each operation then goes on a Roofline chart. In one bug reported in the open-source torch-spyre project , cloning a 65-element fp16 tensor returned a wrong last value. The transfer log was correct, but the compiled copy covered only the first 64 elements, and comparing each layer's output against a reference found the error at that step. Figure 3: The debugging and performance methods taught in Courses 5 and 6, drawn from the open-source torch-spyre debugging and profiling guides. Both walk the same compiler stack. Correctness work looks for the first layer whose output diverges from a reference. Performance work attributes measured time to the layer and memory level that caused it. Figure 4: Roofline analysis as taught in Course 6. A roofline shows how far an operation sits below its bound. It does not show why. On a dataflow target the cause can be scheduling: data shuffling, graph traversal, or pipeline stalls. Profilers localize time to kernels, data transfers, and communication. How finely they attribute time inside a kernel depends on the tool. Labs on Google Colab and Spyre Every course culminates in a core lab that runs on Google Colab with standard PyTorch. Each lab also has an optional Spyre practice portion that runs on Spyre hardware. The labs are developed by Rashed Bhatti, PhD, a senior technical staff member at IBM Research and a contributing lab instructor for the specialization. Each takes 90 minutes to two hours, and students write and run their own code. In the first lab they build a benchmarking harness from scratch with torch.

title: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says
abstract: On Monday, a court granted the US government’s request to deny release of a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a top-secret conference room to steal the frontier lab’s secrets. In a court filing Sunday, US attorney Craig Missakian argued that Abdulrahman Alfozan must continue to be detained while the US makes its case that Alfozan brazenly spied on OpenAI, either for his own personal business gain or to benefit the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Evidence showed that Alfozan had been chatting with a member of the KSA royal family on WhatsApp, while pursuing opportunities to permanently move back to Saudi Arabia during the country’s biggest AI push yet, the government argued. Shortly before his arrest, the FBI found he accessed a folder called “Saudi Gov Docs” on his iPhone, where he also allegedly stored photos of a second bug he planted in the offices. With so much evidence against him, Alfozan—a Saudi national and US permanent legal resident—is a flight risk with seemingly endless support from the Saudi government, Missakian alleged. The FBI arrested Alfozan days before he could hop a plane, Missakian said. The US attorney noted that Alfozan had already booked a one-way ticket for him, his wife, and their baby to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s capital. That ticket was allegedly “paid for by the Saudi government.” Following his arrest, his wife and son booked a sooner flight and immediately left the US without him. Once again, the US found “a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for yet another one-way ticket for the defendant’s wife and son, this one business class to Doha, Qatar.” After receiving “significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area,” Alfozan has “ample resources” to run away to Saudi Arabia, the US government alleged. He also has “at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia,” the government said. To support their request to detain Alfozan, the government pointed to a case where former Twitter employees were charged with spying for the Saudi government . Charges are still pending against one of the ex-Twitter staffers, Ali Alzabarah, the US said, partly because “a Saudi foreign official” helped “coordinate a next-day flight to Saudi Arabia” shortly after Twitter confronted him.

title: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
abstract: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games , with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms . Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely. Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflex , which had been set to go live with today’s launch of Steam Next Fest . In a post on social media Friday evening , the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, “we’re concerned that the demo’s content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game’s presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch.” Instead, the developer now plans to share the demo only in “closed sessions” with those who agree to rules regarding posting and streaming gameplay. Alliance Arts isn’t alone in taking a more defensive stance toward sharing ideas. Papers, Please developer Lucas Pope said on an April podcast that, in general, “you don’t really talk about stuff when you’re working on it because I don’t know it’s going to get slurped up by AI or people are going to copy it or something else like that… I just didn’t feel as comfortable talking about the stuff I was working on again.” Whose game is it, anyway? Concerns about ideas getting “slurped by AI” have been more than theoretical for a number of indie developers in recent months. In March, developer Freya Holmér attracted some viral social media attention after sharing a video of a prototype of a Tetris -style game played on a central rotating pivot point. Days later, Holmér was confronted with a number of vibe-coded copies that made the basic concept widely playable before Holmér could release her own version.

title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
abstract: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry , court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand —potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology , and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations. In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders. The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.

title: I Can See Everything
abstract: Nick Cammarata of Goodfire makes a bold claim: Neural Networks are Already Clean . This was his follow up after various resulting online discussions . This is clearly good work that tells us new and important things. The question is, how big an update is this, how much progress does it represent and what is the outlook going forward? The reactions here range from the super optimistic takes of ‘this means mechanistic interpretability is solvable,’ or even ‘all but solved,’ with comparisons to the famous paper Attention is All You Need . Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): There is so much to say about this, and I will, but WOW, congratulations to Nick and Goodfire. This may be one of the most important single days in deep learning history, and perhaps much more than that. No matter what, this is a victory for the dogged pursuit of understanding. roon (OpenAI): when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even Eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a ‘normal science’ This paper is solid and meaningful contribution that is in some ways overstated. Get excited, but also there are those who need to take a chill pill. We did not actually get an apples-to-apples jump from 1.7% to 90% interpretability of LLM neurons. I interpret Eliezer as slightly lowering his p(doom), but not all that much . Evžen Wybitul : What’s happening? Half of my tl is non-interp people from OAI painting the post as the second coming of Christ and the other half is interp researchers (including Leo Gao) saying it’s… fine This post is my attempt to sort this out. Currently I am landing somewhere in the middle. It is an important update about how LLMs and minds form and operate. It tells us how to go about some useful tasks and reduces our estimate of some task difficulties. Great work, assuming the work checks out. The whole thing very much has a ring of truth, and of a person being curious. You love to see it. What it does not tell us is that interpretability will soon be solved, or is about to be made into a science, let alone that alignment will soon be handled. The hype got rather out of hand in some places. Table of Contents Good Smoke, Potential Fire. One Neuron, One Central Concept. I Can See Everything. What a Concept. The More You Know. Attention Is Still What You Need. Occam’s Razor. The Neurons Sometimes Share Clear Themes. Hype. Anti-Hype. Theme and Variations. Is This How Minds Work? But We Can Open The Box, Said Toad. That Was Not the Hard Problem. More Skepticism. That’s All There Is, There Ain’t No More. The Default Outcome of Mech Interp is Goodhart’s Law. Interpretability is Dual Use. Now The Work Can Begin. Good Smoke, Potential Fire Before I cover reactions or take a side, here are my highlights. It is worth reading at least this much of the primary source. Reading the whole thing is an option, but it is long and the writing can be easy to bounce off of and can repeat itself. Nick Cammarata, Goodfire : The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought. I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. One Neuron, One Central Concept The central claim is that for larger LLMs, most neurons represents a singular concept and things clustered around that concept, perhaps with small offshoots and some use of low-level activations. … Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. … With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. Where previously the working theory was that models overloaded neurons with unrelated concepts in superposition, Nick’s theory is you did not think sufficiently hard to identify the unifying concept. Each neuron is a generalization, mostly ones we can readily understand if we look. … What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place. Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. … So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. … Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. … Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. This pictures intelligence as brute force. Neurons are compound words in German. New concept? Go get another neuron. And yet, it works. I Can See Everything … The bad news about modern neural networks is that they’re enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place. In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. Nick argues that this means that it is easier to solve the full puzzle and understand everything, and then take a measurement of your specific area of interest, then to try to directly pull a fuzzy concept like ‘deception’ out of a pool of mystery neurons. … “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. … All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps. Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them. With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect. Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.
